question.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two continuous random variables with the joint probability density function

$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{x+y}, & x\le 0,\,y\le 0, \\ 0, & \text{otherwise}.\end{aligned}
$$

The marginal CDF ${F}_{Y}(y)$ of $Y$ is given by

$$
{F}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}g(y), & y\le 0 \\ 1 & y>0.\end{aligned}
$$

What is the function $g(y)?$
question.worked_solution:
If $X$ and $Y$ are two continuous random variables with joint probability density function $f(x,y),$ then the marginal density functions for $X$ and $Y$ are

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{X}(x)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}y,\,{f}_{Y}(y)={\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }f(x,y)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

In our case, the marginal density function of $Y$ for $y\le 0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{y}{lim}_{b\to -\infty }{\int }_{b}^{0}{e}^{x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={e}^{y}{lim}_{b\to -\infty }{[{e}^{x}]}_{b}^{0} \\  & ={e}^{y}{lim}_{b\to -\infty }(1-{e}^{b}) \\  & ={e}^{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the marginal CDF of $Y$ for $y\le 0$ is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}_{Y}(y) & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{f}_{Y}(u)\,\text{d}u \\  & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{y}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{b\to -\infty }{\int }_{b}^{y}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={lim}_{b\to -\infty }{[{e}^{u}]}_{b}^{y} \\  & ={lim}_{b\to -\infty }({e}^{y}-{e}^{b}) \\  & ={e}^{y}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the full expression for ${F}_{Y}(y)$ is

$$
{F}_{Y}(y)=\{\begin{aligned}{e}^{y}, & y\le 0 \\ 1 & y>0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, $g(y)={e}^{y}.$
